newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 24.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Monday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* AT&T will begin testing an electronic box that would tie home telephones to its wireless network, advancing the company's effort to offer local phone services nationwide.
* The $17.8 billion merger between SBC and Pacific Telesis Group could be in jeopardy because of California's decision to require SBC to pay customers $750 million.
* American Electric Power is expected to make a bid for Yorkshire Electricity for more than $2 billion.
* Hyatt Hotels plans to spend $1 billion during the next three years to acquire 20 to 30 hotels.
* The U.S., Japan, China, Singapore, Australia and Hong Kong next week plan to launch an Asian counterpart to the Group of Seven.
* Washington Mutual and Norwest are considering "white knight" offers for Great Western Financial, which is fighting an unsolicited $6.05 billion bid from H.F. Ahmanson
* PepsiCo said it expects its international beverage business to return to profitability next year.
* A survey by employment services company Manpower Inc indicates job growth is expected to remain strong in the second quarter.
* Dean Witter employees could hear as early as Monday how many in their ranks will be laid off following the company's merger with Morgan Stanley.
* C-Cube Microsystems plans to reveal a new chip that could lower the cost of video disk players to below $500.
* The Securities and Exchange Commission this week will propose letting mutual funds be sold on "profile" documents before investors get full prospectuses.
* Big Board short interest rose 4.8 percent to 2.94 billion shares in the month that ended in mid-February.
* Revlon's shares rose five percent after financier Ronald Perelman presented a plan to refinance $1.15 billion in debt weighing on the company's stock.
* Chubb is close to selling its life insurance business to Jefferson-Pilot for about $800 million.

* Gordon Crawford, the 50-year-old media investor-analyst extraordinaire of the huge Capital Group mutual funds, prides himself on staying close to luminaries such as Gerald Levin, Barry Diller and Ted Turner. By doing so, he gains valuable information about the industry, and is able to share his knowledge with Wall Street insiders.

This arrangement served Mr. Crawford well when media companies were growing and merging in recent years. With an estimated $10 billion to play with in his heyday -"less now," he says -- he made a ton of money for clients. But did his close ties to insiders make him reluctant to sell? -- Heard on the Street.

* In another sign of bond-market buoyancy, the market for volatile mortgage securities -- which caused huge investor losses and helped fuel the demise of Kidder Peabody & Co during the 1994 bond-market debacle -- is back in a big way. So far this year, investors have snapped up nearly $17 billion of these often-arbitrary bonds. -- Credit Markets.
